Suspecting Mr. Hemani and his family members of terrorism-related activities, the government con- ducted a search of the family home in 2022. Throughout the process, Mr. Hemani proved cooperative: he surrendered a gun he kept in the house, pointed agents to some marijuana on the property, and consented to an interview during which he told law enforcement agents that he used marijuana about every other day. More than six months after the search, and relying solely on Mr. Hemani's admitted use of marijuana, the government prosecuted Mr. Hemani under 18 U. S. The issue before us is whether the court abused its discretion or violated Marichal’s constitutional rights by denying Marichal’s motion to continue after a defense witness did not appear on the date of trial. Marichal told a responding police officer that she had been at a “brew fest” and had consumed alcohol. Marichal also told the officer that she was the driver and sole occupant of the vehicle. The trial was continued several times in 2022 and 2023 for reasons that are not clear from the record. Maine's Minimum Wage to Increase to $15.70 Per Hour in 2027

September 18, 2026

For Immediate Release: September 18, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor announced today that, effective January 1, 2027, the state minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 per hour, based on data recently made available by the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. MDOL is required under Maine law (Maine statute Title 26, chapter 7, section 664) to make annual adjustments to the minimum wage based on the cost-of-living index (CPI-W) for the Northeast Region, after Maine voters amended the law by referendum in 2016. Between August 2025 and August 2026, there was a 4.1 percent increase in the CPI-W.

According to the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey for 2025, there were 28,000 hourly workers who were paid less than $15.00 per hour. These workers represent about four percent of all wage and salary workers (both paid at hourly rates and not paid at hourly rates) and about eight percent of wage and salary workers who are paid at hourly rates.

Agricultural workers in Maine are also entitled to the state minimum wage, after the Legislature enacted and Governor Mills signed "An Act to Establish a State Minimum Hourly Wage for Agricultural Workers" in 2025.

The "tip wage," or service employee minimum wage, will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour. This means that service employees must receive a direct cash wage of at least $7.85 per hour from the employer. The employer must be able to show that the employee receives at least the minimum wage of $15.70 per hour when the direct wage and tips are combined at the end of the week. The amount of tips necessary to qualify as a service employee will increase from $191 to $199 per month.

The minimum salary threshold for exempting a worker from overtime pay must exceed 3,000 times the State's minimum wage or the annualized rate established by the U.S. Department of Labor, whichever is higher. Starting January 1, 2027, the new minimum salary threshold for salaried workers exempt from overtime will be $905.79 per week, or $47,101.08 per year. This is only one of the factors used in determining whether a worker is exempt from overtime pay under federal or state law. An individual can earn more than the minimum salary threshold and still be eligible for overtime. The duties of each worker must be considered as part of this analysis.

Employers can download the required minimum wage poster at no cost on the Department's website.

The minimum wage and overtime law can be found here.

More information about minimum wage and other labor standards is available on the Department's website

ISABELLA COUNTY, MICHIGAN certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the sixth circuit No. 25–95. Argued February 25, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 The Pung family owed $2,241.93 in real-property taxes, so local tax author- ities in Isabella County, Michigan, initiated foreclosure proceedings and sold the Pung home—which was assessed at $194,400 for tax purposes— for $76,008 at public auction. Michael Pung sued in Federal court, and the District Court granted Pung partial summary judgment on his Fifth Amendment claim. The court held that Pung should receive only the surplus proceeds from the tax sale—i. e., the difference between the sale price and the tax debt—not the property's fair market value. The District Court also rejected Pung's claim under the Eighth Amendment Excessive Fines Clause. The Sixth Circuit affrmed. Held: 1. The proper baseline for measuring “just compensation” following a tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property's hypothetical fair market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the country's history of tax sales. Pp. 35–43. (a) For hundreds of years, English and American law have allowed the seizure and sale of property as a tax-collection method, provided that the government return any surplus proceeds to the debtor. LOUISIANA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS AND PUBLIC SAFETY et al. certiorari to the united states court of appeals for the fth circuit No. 23–1197. Argued November 10, 2025—Decided June 23, 2026 The Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act of 2000 (RLUIPA) was enacted pursuant to Congress's Spending Clause author- ity and imposes various conditions on federal funds distributed to state prison systems like the Louisiana Department of Corrections (LDOC). One condition requires state prison systems to agree to answer federal suits by private plaintiffs alleging certain substantial burdens on their re- ligious exercises. See 42 U. S. C. §§ 2000cc–1(a), (b)(1). Relying on that provision, inmate Damon Landor brought this RLUIPA lawsuit against LDOC as well as some of the prison system's individual offcers in their personal capacities, seeking damages from them. Mr. Landor is a Rastafarian whose religious convictions require him to leave his hair uncut. He claims that LDOC offcers—despite being aware of his reli- gious beliefs—forcibly shaved his head. The offcers moved to dismiss, arguing that while their employer LDOC may have agreed to answer cer- tain private suits under RLUIPA, they were not parties to any such agreement, and therefore Mr. Landor had no federal cause of action against them. Hawaii responded by replacing its old law on carry permits with new laws that achieved a similar result. At issue in this case is a Hawaii law that prohibits frearms on private property open to the public without the express and affrmative consent of the property owner. item.content:encoded:
WHEREAS, quality, cost-effective, and patient-centered healthcare is essential to the well-being and quality of life of all people in Maine; and


WHEREAS, physician associates/assistants (PAs) are nationally certified and state-licensed medical professionals who diagnose illnesses, develop and manage treatment plans, prescribe medications, and often serve as a patient's principal healthcare provider; and


WHEREAS, PAs are trusted providers and vital members of the healthcare team, enhancing access to high-quality care in primary care settings, hospitals, rural communities, and underserved areas; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs deliver compassionate, expert care, often serving as the first point of contact for patients and empowering individuals and families to be active participants in their own health; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs provide critical care across a broad range of medical specialties, including addressing the growing demand for behavioral and mental health services by offering compassionate, evidence-based care to individuals and families in need; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs are committed to addressing health disparities, expanding access, and providing team-based, person-centered care across every medical specialty and setting; and
 

WHEREAS, PAs have earned the respect of patients and colleagues alike for their clinical excellence, adaptability, and deep dedication to the communities they serve; and
 

WHEREAS, Maine has been a leader in progressing PA practice and ensuring access to PA services by enacting legislation in recent years to join the PA compact, change the title of the profession to accurately reflect the scope of the profession, and allow PAs to practice at the top of their education and training;


NOW, THEREFORE, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim October 6-12, 2026 as 

National PA Week

in Maine, and I encourage all residents to recognize and celebrate the important role that PAs play in improving health, advancing equity, and delivering high-quality care across the healthcare system.

In testimony whereof, I have caused

the Great Seal of the State to be

hereunto affixed GIVEN under my

hand at Augusta this twenty ninth day of

September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

item.title: 806 Nonresident Individual Income Tax (PDF)
item.description:
18 DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE AND FINANCIAL SERVICES
125 BUREAU OF REVENUE SERVICES INCOME/ESTATE TAX DIVISION
Chapter 806: NONRESIDENT INDIVIDUAL INCOME TAX
SUMMARY: This rule provides income tax guidance for nonresident individuals in the following areas:
• Determination of Maine-source income; • Deduction of Maine losses; • Attribution and apportionment of income, tax additions and tax credits to Maine; • Returns, worksheets and schedules to be used for filing; • Determination of taxable income and tax credits for spouses filing as single individuals; and • Income tax withholding obligations.
Outline of Contents:
.01 Definitions .02 Income subject to Maine income tax .03 Income not subject to Maine income tax .04 Deduction of losses .05 Special sourcing rules .06 Income tax credits .07 Return of nonresident or part-year resident individual .08 Maine taxable income computation for spouses filing as single individuals .09 Maine tax additions and tax credits for spouses filing as single individuals .10 Maine income tax withholding obligations .11 Application date
.01 Definitions. As used in this rule, unless the context otherwise indicates or may otherwise require, the following terms have the following meanings that shall apply throughout the rule.
A. Code. “Code” means the United States Internal Revenue Code of 1986 and amendments to that Code as of the date stated in 36 M.R.S. § 111(1-A).
18-125 Chapter 806 page 2
B. Intangible property. “Intangible property” means a right or possession of a nonphysical or abstract nature that has value, or a financial asset that has no intrinsic value but that represents value. Intangible property includes, but is not limited to, copyrights, patents, licenses, bills of exchange, trademarks, business books and records, business goodwill, covenants not to compete, securities, bonds, notes, insurance policies, and accounts receivable.

Title IV PostsecondaryInstitutions: Workforce Pell Program Applications Open for Second Review Cycle Through Nov. 13

October 14, 2026

For Immediate Release

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist | media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA -The State Workforce Development Board(SWDB) is accepting applications from Title IV postsecondary institutionsseeking stateapproval to offer programs eligible for federal Workforce Pell Grants. Applications for the second review cycle are due Friday, Nov. 13

Maine's Workforce Pell application provides an online process for eligible postsecondary institutions to seek approval to offer short-term workforce training programs that meet federal Workforce Pell Grant requirements. Applications are accepted on a rolling basis and reviewed quarterly by the SWDB.

Workforce Pell expands federal Pell Grant eligibility to approved short-term workforce training programs that prepare students for high-skill, high-wage and in-demand careers. States are responsible for reviewing and certifying eligible programs before they are submitted to the U.S. Department of Education for final approval.

"Workforce Pell opens the door to new education and career opportunities for more people across our state,"said Vaughan Woodruff, chair of the State Workforce Development Board."The program's support for training that connects people with skills needed for Maine's workforce presents a significant opportunity for Maine workers and employers."

The Maine Workforce Pell Program Determination Policy establishesthe state's process foridentifying, reviewing and recommending eligible short-term workforce training programs for Workforce Pell. The policy was developed in partnership with the Maine Department of Labor, Maine Department of Education, Finance Authority of Maine, Maine Community College System and University of MaineSystem.

"Workforce Pell brings a new source of federal funding to Maine's short-term workforce training programs," said Maine Department of Labor Commissioner Laura Fortman. "We are excited to help Maine's postsecondary institutions take advantage of this opportunity to strengthen their programs, reach more students and prepare Maine's workforce for the future."

The SWDB will evaluate applications and make recommendations to the Governor for state certification. Programs certified by the Governor will then be submitted to the U.S. Department of Education for final approval. Following federal approval, the SWDB will publish the list of Maine-certified Workforce Pell programs on the Maine Workforce Pell webpage within 30 days.

Institutions can find the Workforce Pell application, eligibility requirements, program guidance and additional information on the Maine Workforce Pell webpage.

Pursuant to an agreement with the State, Reardon pleaded guilty to domestic violence assault on the condition that if he successfully complied with the deferment requirements , then he would be permitted to withdraw his guilty plea and instead plead guilty to a charge of domestic violence reckless conduct. At a final hearing following the deferment period, the trial court (Piscataquis County, Larson, J.) found that Reardon had failed to comply with certain deferment requirements but that his failure to comply was excusable. The court nonetheless concluded, relying on principles of contract interpretation, that Reardon was not entitled to the successful 2 outcome of the agreement and accordingly entered a judgment of conviction for domestic violence assault. item.title: Standing Order: Standing Order Requiring Paper Filing for Election Day 2026 Emergency Matters
item.description:
STATE OF MAINE SUPERIOR COURT DISTRICT COURT
STANDING ORDER REQUIRING PAPER FILING FOR ELECTION DAY 2026 EMERGENCY MATTERS
The Maine Judicial Branch (MJB) is implementing the Maine eCourts system – including eFiling – statewide.1 EFileMaine is a practical and efficient document submission system already in use in many courts throughout the state. However, because filings related to Election Day may be uniquely time- sensitive, to ensure timely processing, the MJB will require paper filing under the limited circumstances described below.
It is therefore ORDERED that any emergency Title 21-A filings related to Election Day 2026 filed between 4:00 p.m. on Friday, October 30, 2026, and 9:00 p.m. on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, must be by paper, unless otherwise ordered.2
It is further ORDERED that the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems are SUSPENDED to the extent necessary to give effect to this order.
Dated: 10/28/2026 _____/s/______________________ Chief Justice Robert E. Mullen
Dated: 10/28/2026 ___/s/_______________________ Chief Judge Brent Davis
1 Further information about the Maine eCourts system is available at https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html 2 Any Election Day 2026 filings filed by eFile during this period may not be processed until the next business day after the election.

item.title: Federal Financial Participation in State Assistance Expenditures; Federal Matching Shares for Medicaid, the Children's Health Insurance Program, and Aid to Needy Aged, Blind, or Disabled Persons for October 1, 2027, Through September 30, 2028
item.description: The Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (FMAP) and Enhanced Federal Medical Assistance Percentages (eFMAP) for fiscal year 2028 have been calculated pursuant to the Social Security Act (the Act). These percentages will be effective from October 1, 2027, through September 30, 2028. This notice announces the calculated FMAP rates, in accordance with the Act, that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will use in determining the amount of Federal matching for State medical assistance (Medicaid), Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) Contingency Funds, Child Support collections, Child Care Mandatory and Matching Funds of the Child Care and Development Fund, Title IV-E Foster Care Maintenance payments, Adoption Assistance payments and Kinship Guardianship Assistance payments, and the eFMAP rates for the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) expenditures. Table 1 gives figures for each of the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands. This notice reminds states of adjustments available for states meeting requirements for disproportionate employer pension or insurance fund contributions and adjustments for disaster recovery. At this time, no state qualifies for such adjustments, and territories are not eligible.

item.title: Agencies Announce Dollar Thresholds for Applicability of Truth in Lending and Consumer Leasing Rules for Consumer Credit and Lease Transactions
item.description: The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing). By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations. Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan. Read the Consumer Leasing (Regulation M) Read the Truth in Lending (Regulation Z) Media Contacts: CFPB: press@cfpb.gov FRB: Chelsea Grate, (202) 452-2955 Page last modified Nov. 25, 2026 @ 03:00 PM EST
item.content:encoded:
The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing).

By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations.

Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.
